correctness.rationale: The distinct slopes and finite collision parameters give the fifteen ordinary nodes and ten different finite singular fibers. At the smooth point on the distinguished branch line the pencil is locally [u:w²] on the double cover; two blowups resolve the map. The first exceptional strict transform is a multiplicity-one arm met by the second exceptional (the section), and the branch line becomes a square −3 multiplicity-two curve. The five other arms are the square −2 exceptional curves at its nodes. A finite collision has one square −2 exceptional component and an irreducible normalized proper transform, as in Bannai–Tokunaga. Removing the arm met by the section gives the matrix with leaf block −2I₅, central entry −3, and cross entries 1. The Schur complement is −1/2, hence determinant 16. The fiber and section block is unimodular and the ten finite nonidentity blocks contribute 2^10, giving rank 18 and absolute discriminant 2^14. Clingher–Malmendier–Shaska Prop. 3.2 gives the generic rank-six transcendental lattice of absolute discriminant 2^6; two blowups give NS rank 18 with the same absolute discriminant. The quotient therefore has order 16. Independently of the exact wording of the citation to Shioda, divisor restriction onto the generic fiber is surjective by closure on the regular surface (a K-point identifies the rational Picard group with line-bundle classes); the kernel is vertical after subtracting a principal divisor. Removing the degree via O and using Pic=NS gives exactly the asserted quotient. The full 16-element two-torsion is rational because all branch points are rational. Consequently 2P~2O for any rational P; the divisor 2P lies in the hyperelliptic pencil and is a doubled ramification point. This proves the exact group and six-point census in the stated regime.
residual_risks: The generic Picard lattice is an external geometric input, not certified by the finite checker. No conclusion is drawn for Picard-jump configurations or pencils with collided directions. Exact wording of Shioda's Theorem 2.1 was not verified from a readable full text; direct restriction proves the needed assertion here.
